category_title: Students exhibiting conflict avoidance in collaborative group work
minimal_context: During a class session in an honors seminar, the tutor asks Joey to publicly share a metaphor describing his research team's progress with his peers.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Joey, please go ahead and publicly share the metaphor you wrote to describe your research team and your progress.

STUDENT: I described my team as an engine. This engine runs really well on three cylinders, but when the other two spark plug wires are attached, the engine acts almost as if it is supercharged.

TUTOR: What does that mean for your group's dynamics?

STUDENT: Up to this point the engine is running really well but there is so much more performance possible when all the spark plug wires contribute spark.

TUTOR: This is an opportunity to encourage your teammates to become more engaged with the project. Do you have anything else to add about the deadlines or participation?

STUDENT: (Looks uncomfortable) No, we are having relative success. I just want to encourage everyone to fully engage in the research process. Everything is fine.

options.A: Meet individually with the student who disclosed frustrations about the research team, discuss strategies for contributing, acknowledge and normalize emotional responses, and problem-solve labor distribution.
options.B: Provide specific praise statements immediately after the student's specific behavior during the public sharing of the metaphor with the seminar peers.
options.C: Ask all three types of follow-up questions (inference, justify, opinion) within the same exchange regarding the student's metaphor about the research team.
options.D: Produce authoritativeness by speaking in short sentences, like headlines in a newspaper; talk briefly and concisely, mentioning only main details about the research team.
